courses.title: Tutorial and Seminar in Psychiatry
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: conduct clinical teaching for tutorials and seminar and emergency teaching based on the principle of courses outlined in PSY 601 to 603 above; and
lay emphasis on the must know desired competencies and common psychiatric disorders
courses.contents: Clinical teaching for tutorials and seminar and emergency teaching based on the principle of courses outlined in PSY 601 to 603 above. Emphasis on the must know desired competencies and common psychiatric disorders.

courses.title: Plastic Surgery and Burns
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: list symptoms and signs of common lesions in plastic and reconstructive surgery;
discuss principles of management of common lesions in plastic and reconstructive surgery;
investigate patients;
treat; and
manage complications.
courses.contents: Symptoms and signs of common lesions in plastic and reconstructive surgery, including their interpretations. Introduction to principles of management of common lesions in plastic and reconstructive surgery (ulcers, burns and skin grafts.) including relevant investigations, treatment, and treatment complications. Cleft lip and palate. Common cutaneous lesions and cosmetic surgery.

courses.title: Cardiothoracic including Vascular Surgery
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: enumerate symptoms and signs of common lesions in cardiothoracic and vascular surgery;
discuss chest trauma and chest wall tumours;
explain principles of management of common lesions in cardiothoracic surgery;
investigate, treat and manage complications; and
list congenital malformations and their management.
courses.contents: Symptoms and signs of common lesions in cardiothoracic and vascular surgery, including their interpretations. Chest trauma and chest wall tumours. Introduction to principles of management of common lesions in cardiothoracic surgery including relevant investigations, treatment and complications. Congenital malformations and their management.

courses.title: Neurosurgery
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: discuss head injury and spinal trauma;
enumerate common surgical intracranial lesions and spinal cord lesions;
discuss congenital malformations and management; and
appraise the neurosurgical patient and intracranial haemorrhage.
courses.contents: Head injury and spinal trauma. Common surgical intracranial lesions as well as spinal cord lesions. Congenital malformations and their management. Evaluation of the neurosurgical patient and intracranial haemorrhage.

courses.title: Special Topics in Surgery
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: enumerate general principles;
explain acutely injured, poly-traumatised patient;
discuss mass casualty; and
explain fractures and dislocations.
courses.contents: General principles. Acutely injured, poly-traumatised patient. Mass casualty. Fractures and dislocations.

courses.title: Clinics, Theatre and Call Duty Bed Side Teaching
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: conduct clinical evaluation according to the principles of SUG 605 to 611.
courses.contents: Clinical evaluation according to the principles of SUG 605 to 611.

courses.title: Metabolic and Endocrine Medicine
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate sound theoretical knowledge of the subject;
list and display clinical skills in the evaluation of the metabolic and endocrine patient;
investigate patients with utmost prioritisation;
manage and prevent the disease as may be applicable; and
exhibit sound knowledge of individual and community level prevention of diseases.
courses.contents: Diabetes mellitus. Risk factors. Pathogenesis. Clinical features and presentations. Complications. Investigations. Management. Hypothalamic. Pituitary. Adrenal-thyroid axis. Disorders of the hypothalamus. Disorders of the pituitary gland. Disorders of the thyroid gland. Disorders of calcium metabolism. Inborn errors of metabolism. Gout and wilson’s disease.

courses.title: Neurology II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate sound theoretical knowledge of the subject;
list and display sound clinical skills in the evaluation of the neurology patient;
investigate patients with utmost prioritisation;
manage and prevent the disease as may be applicable; and
offer appropriate health education.
courses.contents: Higher cerebral function and dementia. Stroke. Sleep. Epilepsy. Parkinson’s disease. Headache. spinal cord lesions. Peripheral neuropathy. Neuro-musculoskeletal diseases. Myasthenia gravis. Muscular dystrophy. The cranial nerves and autonomic neuropathy. Coma (causes, management). Meningitis (CSM, H. influenza, tuberculosis, pneumococcal). Viral infections of CNS. Cerebral abscess. Demyelinating disease. Cord compression. Brain tumours. Subacute combined degeneration.

courses.title: Cardiology II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate sound theoretical knowledge of the subject;
list and display sound clinical skills in the evaluation of the cardiac patient;
investigate patients with utmost prioritisation;
demonstrate the knowledge and skills to manage and prevent the disease; and
identify risk factors, individual and community level for CVD.
courses.contents: Pathological functional sates of the heart: systolic and diastolic dysfunction; arrhythmias; ischaemic heart diseases. Cardiomyopathies. Dilated, restrictive and hypertrophic. Peripheral vascular diseases. Acute and chronic arterial diseases, embolic diseases, venous thromboembolism. CVS infections. Congenital abnormalities. Valvular abnormalities. Emergencies in cardiology.

courses.title: Gastroenterology II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate sound theoretical knowledge of the subject;
list and display sound clinical skills in the evaluation of the gastroenterology patient;
investigate patients with utmost prioritisation;
manage and prevent the disease as may be applicable; and
exhibit sound knowledge of individual and community level prevention of diseases.
courses.contents: Peptic ulcer disease. Cholecystitis and pancreatitis with consideration of diagnostic procedure such as laboratory tests. Cholecystogram. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). Chronic active hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. Gastrointestinal bleeding. Gastrointestinal malignancies. Malabsorption syndromes. Hepatic failure.

courses.title: Rheumatology and Care of the Elderly
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate sound theoretical knowledge of the subject;
list and display sound clinical skills in the evaluation of the patient;
investigate patients with utmost prioritisation;
manage and prevent the disease as may be applicable; and
exhibit sound knowledge of individual and community level prevention of diseases.
courses.contents: The sero-negative arthritides. The sero-positive arthritides. Rheumatoid arthritis, sjogren’s syndrome, ankylosing spondylitis, enteropathic arthropathy, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease). The connective tissue disorders. Systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), mixed connective tissue disease, dermatomyositis/polymyositis, giant cell arteritis, lessons on rehabilitation. Physiological and psychosocial changes in old age, medical and surgical diseases of the elderly. Psychiatric disorders of the elderly. Nutrition in the elderly. Competence and forensic issues in the elderly.

courses.title: Haematology II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate sound theoretical knowledge of the subject;
list and display sound clinical skills in the evaluation of the patient;
investigate patients with utmost prioritisation;
manage and prevent the disease as may be applicable; and
exhibit sound knowledge of individual and community level prevention of diseases.
courses.contents: Anaemias. Nutritional. Haemolytic. Aplastic. Haemoglobinopathies. Bleeding disorders. Haematological manifestations of chronic diseases. Myelo-proliferative disorders/leukaemia’s. Lymphomas. Myelomatosis.

courses.title: Infectious Diseases II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate sound theoretical knowledge of the subject;
list and display sound clinical skills in the evaluation of the patient;
investigate patients with utmost prioritisation;
manage and prevent the disease as may be applicable; and
exhibit sound knowledge of individual and community level prevention of diseases.
courses.contents: Host-pathogen interactions. Sepsis, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), and multi-organ dysfunction syndrome. Viral infectious syndromes. Anaerobic infectious syndromes. Non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections. Diagnosis and treatment of Fungal infections. Infections complicating animal bites.

courses.title: Nephrology II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate sound theoretical knowledge of the subject;
list and display sound clinical skills in the evaluation of the patient;
investigate patients with utmost prioritisation;
manage and prevent the disease as may be applicable; and
exhibit sound knowledge of individual and community level prevention of diseases.
courses.contents: Glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome. Acute Kidney injury. Acute drug poisoning and overdose. Chronic kidney disease. Dialysis-acute and chronic. Urinary tract infection. Hypertension. Nephrolithiasis. Renal transplantation – indications. Post-surgical management, rejection and its management.

courses.title: Pulmonology II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate sound theoretical knowledge of the subject;
list and display sound clinical skills in the evaluation of the patient;
investigate patients with utmost prioritisation;
manage and prevent the disease as may be applicable; and
exhibit sound knowledge of individual and community level prevention of diseases.
courses.contents: Respiratory tract infections. Bacterial-pneumonias. Tuberculosis (pulmonary and extrapulmonary). Viral respiratory tract infections. Chronic obstructive lung diseases. Bronchial Asthma. Respiratory failure. Carcinoma of the lungs. Cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis. The pneumoconiosis.

courses.title: Clinics, Call Duty and Bed Side Teaching
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: conduct clinical evaluation according to the principles of MED 601 to 620;
demonstrate hands-on clinical evaluation of specific patients;
conduct history taking, examination, investigation and treatment; and
monitor hospitalised patients.
courses.contents: Clinical evaluation according to the principles of 601-609. Hands on clinical evaluation of specific patients, history, examination, investigation and treatment. Monitoring of hospitalised patients.

courses.title: Communication in English
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: identify possible sound patterns in English language;
list notable language skills;
classify word formation processes;
construct simple and fairly complex sentences in English;
apply logical and critical reasoning skills for meaningful presentations;
demonstrate an appreciable level of the art of public speaking and listening; and
write simple and technical reports.
courses.contents: Sound patterns in English language (phonetics and phonology, vowels and consonants). English word classes (lexical and grammatical words, definitions, forms, functions, usages, collocations). Sentence in English (types: structural and functional, simple and complex). Grammar and usage (tense, mood, modality, concord and aspects of language use in everyday life). Logical and critical thinking and reasoning methods (Logic and syllogism, inductive and deductive argument and reasoning methods, analogy, generalisation and explanations). Ethical considerations, copyright rules and infringements. Writing activities: (Pre-writing, writing, post writing/editing and proofreading; paragraphing, types of writing, summary, essays, letters, curriculum vitae, report writing, note making. and mechanics of writing). Comprehension strategies (reading and types of reading, comprehension skills, 3RsQ). Information and communication technology in modern language learning. Language skills for effective communication. Major word formation processes. Writing and reading comprehension strategies. Logical and critical reasoning for meaningful presentations. Art of public speaking and listening.

courses.title: Nigerian Peoples and Culture
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of the course, students should be able to:
outcomes: analyse the historical foundation of the Nigerian culture and arts in pre-colonial times;
list and identify the major linguistic groups in Nigeria;
explain the gradual evolution of Nigeria as a political unit;
analyse the concepts of trade, economic and self-reliance status of the Nigerian people towards national development;
enumerate the challenges of the Nigerian State towards nation building;
analyse the role of the judiciary in upholding people’s fundamental rights;
identify acceptable norms and values of the major ethnic groups in Nigeria; and
list and suggest possible solutions to identifiable Nigerian environmental, moral and value problems.
courses.contents: Nigerian history, culture, and art up to 1800 (Yoruba, Hausa and Igbo peoples and culture; peoples and culture of the ethnic minority groups). Nigeria under colonial rule (advent of colonial rule in Nigeria, Colonial administration of Nigeria). Evolution of Nigeria as a political unit (amalgamation of Nigeria in 1914, formation of political parties in Nigeria, nationalist movement and struggle for independence). Nigeria and challenges of nation building (military intervention in Nigerian politics and Nigerian Civil War). Concept of trade and economics of self-reliance (indigenous trade and market system, indigenous apprenticeship system among Nigeria people, trade, skill acquisition and self-reliance). Social justices and national development (law, definition and classification). Judiciary and fundamental rights. Individual norms and values (basic Nigeria norms and values, patterns of citizenship acquisition, citizenship and civic responsibilities, indigenous languages, usage and development, negative attitudes and conducts. Cultism, kidnapping and other related social vices). Re-orientation, moral and national values (The 3R’s, reconstruction, rehabilitation and re-orientation). Re- orientation strategies, Operation Feed the Nation (OFN), Green Revolution, Austerity Measures, War Against Indiscipline (WAI), War Against Indiscipline and Corruption (WAIC), Mass Mobilization for Self-Reliance, Social Justice and Economic Recovery (MAMSER), National Orientation Agency (NOA). Current socio-political and cultural developments in Nigeria.

courses.title: Elementary Mathematic I (Algebra and Trigonometry)
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of the course, students should be able to:
outcomes: explain basic definition of set, subsets, union, intersection, complements and use of Venn diagrams;
solve quadratic equations;
solve trigonometric functions;
identify various types of numbers; and
solve some problems using binomial theorem.
courses.contents: Elementary set theory, subsets, union, intersection, complements, Venn diagrams. Real numbers, integers, rational and irrational numbers, mathematical induction, real sequences and series, theory of quadratic equations, binomial theorem. Complex numbers, algebra of complex numbers, the Argand diagram. De-Moivre’s theorem, nth roots of unity. Circular measure, trigonometric functions of angles of any magnitude, addition and factor formulae.

courses.title: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of the course, students should be able to:
outcomes: identify types of rules in differentiation and integration;
describe the meaning of function of a real variable, graphs, limits and continuity; and
solve some applications of definite integrals in areas and volumes.
courses.contents: Function of a real variable, graphs, limits and idea of continuity. The derivative, as limit of rate of change. Techniques of differentiation. Extreme curve sketching, integration as an inverse of differentiation. Methods of integration and definite integrals. Application to areas and volumes.

courses.title: General Biology I
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of lectures in Plant Biology, students should be able to:
outcomes: explain cells structure and organisations;
summarise functions of cellular organelles;
characterise living organisms and state their general reproduction;
describe the interrelationship that exists between organisms;
discuss the concept of heredity and evolution; and
enumerate habitat types and their characteristics.
courses.contents: Cell structure and organisation. Functions of cellular organelles. Characteristics and classification of living things. Chromosomes, genes their relationships and importance. General reproduction. Interrelationships of organisms (competitions, parasitism, predation, symbiosis, commensalisms, mutualism, saprophytism). Heredity and evolution (introduction to Darwinism and Lamarkism, Mendelian laws, explanation of key genetic terms). Elements of ecology and types of habitat.

courses.title: General Biology II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of the lectures, students should be able to:
outcomes: list the characteristics, methods of identification and classification of viruses, bacteria and fungi;
state the unique characteristics of plant and animal kingdoms;
describe ecological adaptations in the plant and animal kingdoms;
explain nutrition, respiration, excretion and reproduction in plants and animals; and
describe growth and development in plants and animals.
courses.contents: Basic characteristics, identification and classification of viruses, bacteria and fungi. A generalised survey of the plant and animal kingdoms based mainly on the study of similarities and differences in the external features. Ecological adaptations. Briefs on physiology to include nutrition, respiration, circulatory systems, excretion, reproduction, growth and development.

courses.title: General Biology Practical I
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of the course, students should be able to:
outcomes: outline common laboratory hazards;
provide precautions on laboratory hazards;
state the functions of the different parts of microscope;
use the microscope and describe its maintenance;
draw biological diagrams and illustrations; and
apply scaling and proportion to biological diagrams.
courses.contents: Common laboratory hazards. Prevention and first aid. Measurements in biology. Uses and care of microscope. Compound and dissecting microscope. Biological drawings and illustration, scaling, accuracy and proportion. use of common laboratory apparatus and laboratory experiments designed to illustrate the topics covered in BIO 101.

courses.title: General Biology Practical II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of the course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe the anatomy of flowering plants;
differentiate types of fruit and seeds;
state ways of handling and caring for biological wares;
describe the basic histology of animal tissues; and
identify various groups in the animal kingdom.
courses.contents: Anatomy of flowering plants, primary vegetative body, stem, leaf and root to show the mature tissues namely parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem and phloem. Types of fruits and seeds. Care and use of dissecting kits and other biological wares. Dissection and general histology of animal tissues based on vertebrate forms. Morphology and functions of epithelial, muscular, nervous and connective tissues. Examination of various groups of lower invertebrates under microscopes, identification of various groups of organisms in animal kingdom. And any experiment designed to emphasise the practical aspects of topics in BIO 102.

courses.title: General Chemistry I
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: define atom, molecules and chemical reactions;
discuss the modern electronic theory of atoms;
write electronic configurations of elements on the periodic table;
justify the trends of atomic radii, ionisation energies, electronegativity of the elements based on their position in the periodic table;
identify and balance oxidation – reduction equation and solve redox titration problems;
illustrate shapes of simple molecules and hybridized orbitals;
identify the characteristics of acids, bases and salts and solve problems based on their quantitative relationship;
apply the principles of equilibrium to aqueous systems using LeChatelier’s principle to predict the effect of concentration, pressure and temperature changes on equilibrium mixtures;
analyse and perform calculations with the thermodynamic functions, enthalpy, entropy and free energy; and
determine rates of reactions and its dependence on concentration, time and temperature.
courses.contents: Atoms, molecules, elements, compounds and chemical reactions. Modern electronic theory of atoms. Electronic configuration, periodicity and building up of the periodic table. Hybridisation and shapes of simple molecules. Valence forces and structure of solids. Chemical equations and stoichiometry, chemical bonding and intermolecular forces and kinetic theory of matter. Elementary thermochemistry, rates of reaction, equilibrium and thermodynamics. Acids, bases and salts. Properties of gases. Redox reactions and introduction to electrochemistry. Radioactivity.

courses.title: General Chemistry II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: state the importance and development of organic chemistry;
define fullerenes and its applications;
discuss electronic theory;
determine the qualitative and quantitative of structures in organic chemistry;
describe rules guiding nomenclature and functional group classes of organic chemistry;
determine rate of reaction to predict mechanisms of reaction;
identify classes of organic functional group with brief description of their chemistry;
discuss comparative chemistry of group 1A, IIA and IVA elements; and
describe basic properties of transition metals.
courses.contents: Historical survey of the development and importance of organic chemistry, fullerenes as fourth allotrope of carbon, uses as nanotubules, nanostructures and nano chemistry. Electronic theory in organic chemistry. Isolation and purification of organic compounds. Determination of structures of organic compounds including qualitative and quantitative analysis in organic chemistry. Nomenclature and functional group classes of organic compounds. Introductory reaction mechanism and kinetics. Stereochemistry. The chemistry of alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, alcohols, ethers, amines, alkyl halides, nitriles, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and derivatives. The chemistry of selected metals and non-metals. Comparative chemistry of group IA, IIA and IVA elements. Introduction to transition metal chemistry.

courses.title: General Chemistry Practical I
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe the general laboratory rules and safety procedures;
collect scientific data and correctly carrying out chemical experiment;
identify the basic glassware and equipment in the laboratory;
tell the differences between primary and secondary standards;
perform redox titration;
record observations and measurements in the laboratory notebooks; and
analyse data to arrive at scientific conclusions.
courses.contents: Laboratory experiments designed to reflect topics presented in courses CHM 101 and CHM 102. Acid-base titrations, qualitative analysis, redox reactions, gravimetric analysis, data analysis and presentation.

courses.title: General Chemistry Practical II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, the students should be able to:
outcomes: identify the general laboratory rules and safety procedures;
collect scientific data and correctly carry out chemical experiments;
classify the basic glassware and equipment in the laboratory;
carry out preliminary tests, ignition, boiling point, melting point, test on known and unknown organic compounds;
execute solubility tests on known and unknown organic compounds;
list elemental tests on known and unknown compounds; and
conduct functional group/confirmatory test on known and unknown compounds which could be acidic, basic, neutral organic compounds.
courses.contents: Continuation of CHM 107. Additional laboratory experiments, functional group analysis, quantitative analysis using volumetric methods.

courses.title: General Physics I (Mechanics)
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: identify and deduce the physical quantities and their units;
differentiate between vectors and scalars;
describe and evaluate motion of systems on the basis of the fundamental laws of mechanics;
apply Newton’s laws to describe and solve simple problems of motion;
evaluate work, energy, velocity, momentum, acceleration, and torque of moving or rotating objects;
explain and apply the principles of conservation of energy, linear and angular momentum;
describe the laws governing motion under gravity; and
explain motion under gravity and quantitatively determine behaviour of objects moving under gravity.
courses.contents: Space and time, units and dimension, vectors and scalars, differentiation of vectors: displacement, velocity and acceleration, kinematics, Newton laws of motion (Inertial frames, Impulse, force and action at a distance and momentum conservation). Relative motion, application of Newtonian mechanics, equations of motion, conservation principles in physics, conservative forces, conservation of linear momentum, kinetic energy and work, potential energy, system of particles, centre of mass, rotational motion, torque, vector product, moment, rotation of coordinate axes and angular momentum. Polar coordinates, conservation of angular momentum, circular motion, moments of inertia, gyroscopes and precession. Gravitation, Newton’s Law of gravitation, Kepler’s Laws of planetary motion, gravitational potential energy, escape velocity, satellites motion and orbits.

courses.title: General Physics II (Electricity and Magnetism)
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe the electric field and potential and related concepts, for stationary charges;
calculate electrostatic properties of simple charge distribution using Coulomb’s law, Gauss’s law and electric potential;
describe and determine the magnetic field for steady and moving charges;
determine the magnetic properties of simple current distributions using Biot-Savart and Ampere’s law;
describe electromagnetic induction and related concepts and make calculations using Faraday and Lenz’s laws;
explain the basic physical of Maxwell’s equations in integral form;
evaluate DC circuits to determine the electrical parameters; and
determine the characteristics of ac voltages and currents in resistors, capacitors and inductors.
courses.contents: Forces in nature. Electrostatics. Electric charge and its properties. Methods of charging. Coulomb’s law and superposition. Electric field and potential. Gauss’s law. Capacitance. Electric dipoles. Energy in electric fields. Conductors and insulators. Current, voltage and resistance. Ohm’s law and analysis of DC circuits. Magnetic fields. Lorentz force. Biot-Savart and Ampère’s laws. Magnetic dipoles. Dielectrics, energy in magnetic fields. Electromotive force. Electromagnetic induction. Self and mutual inductances. Faraday and Lenz’s laws. Step up and step down transformers. Maxwell's equations. Electromagnetic oscillations and waves. AC voltages and currents applied to inductors. Capacitors, resistance and combinations.

courses.title: General Practical Physics I
courses.outcomes_intro: On Completion of the course, students should be able to:
outcomes: conduct measurements of some physical quantities;
make observations of events, collect and tabulate data;
identify and evaluate some common experimental errors;
plot and analyse graphs; and
draw conclusions from numerical and graphical analysis of data.
courses.contents: This introductory course emphasises quantitative measurements, the treatment of measurement errors and graphical analysis. A variety of experimental techniques should be employed. The experiments include studies of meters, the oscilloscope, mechanical systems, electrical and mechanical resonant systems, light, heat, viscosity, covered in PHY 101. However, emphasis should be placed on the basic physical techniques for observation, measurements, data collection, analysis and deduction.

courses.title: General Practical Physics II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: conduct measurements of some physical quantities;
make observations of events, collect and tabulate data;
identify and evaluate some common experimental errors;
plot and analyse graphs;
draw conclusions from numerical and graphical analysis of data; and
prepare and present practical reports.
courses.contents: This introductory course emphasises quantitative measurements, the treatment of measurement errors and graphical analysis. A variety of experimental techniques should be employed. The experiments include studies of meters, the oscilloscope, mechanical systems, electrical and mechanical resonant systems, light, heat, viscosity, covered in PHY 102. However, emphasis should be placed on the basic physical techniques for observation, measurements, data collection, analysis and deduction. 200 Level

courses.title: Entrepreneurship and Innovation
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: explain the concepts and theories of entrepreneurship, intrapreneurship, opportunity seeking, new value creation, and risk taking;
state the characteristics of an entrepreneur;
analyse the importance of micro and small businesses in wealth creation, employment and financial independence;
engage in entrepreneurial thinking;
identify key elements in innovation;
describe stages in enterprise formation, partnership and networking including business planning;
describe contemporary entrepreneurial issues in Nigeria, Africa and the rest of the world; and
state the basic principles of e-commerce.
courses.contents: Concept of entrepreneurship (entrepreneurship, intrapreneurship/corporate entrepreneurship). Theories, rationale and relevance of entrepreneurship (schumpeterian and other perspectives, risk-taking, necessity and opportunity-based entrepreneurship and creative destruction). Characteristics of entrepreneurs (opportunity seeker, risk taker, natural and nurtured, problem solver and change agent, innovator and creative thinker). Entrepreneurial thinking (critical thinking, reflective thinking, and creative thinking). Innovation (concept of innovation, dimensions of innovation, change and innovation, knowledge and innovation). Enterprise formation, partnership and networking (basics of business plan, forms of business ownership, business registration and forming alliances and joint ventures). Contemporary entrepreneurship issues (knowledge, skills and technology, intellectual property, virtual office, networking). Entrepreneurship in Nigeria (biography of inspirational entrepreneurs, youth and women entrepreneurship, entrepreneurship support institutions, youth enterprise networks and environmental and cultural barriers to entrepreneurship). Basic principles of e-commerce.

courses.title: Introductory Anatomy, Gross Anatomy of Upper Limbs
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: classify the basic divisions of anatomy into regional, systemic and applied anatomy;
demonstrate knowledge of anatomical terms, anatomical positions, planes, relationships and comparisons, laterality and movement;
identify the shape, two ends, bony markings, and relations of surfaces of the clavicle;
identify the articular surfaces, types, capsules, ligaments and neurovascular supply to the SC and AC joints;
identify the articular surfaces, shaft and bony markings of the Humerus;
identify the articular surfaces, type, joint capsule, extrinsic and extrinsic ligaments and neurovascular supply to the shoulder joint;
describe the ends, articular surfaces, shafts, bony markings and processes of the two forearm bones;
identify the shape, boundaries and contents of the axilla;
describe the articular surfaces, type, capsule, ligaments, range of movement and neurovascular supply of the elbow joint;
describe the attachment and orientation of the fibers of the interosseous membrane;
identify the names, relations and articulations of the two rows of carpal bones;
identify the shapes, bases and heads of metatarsals and their articulations;
discuss the attachments, actions and innervations of the axioappendicular and scapulohumeral muscles;
differentiate the boundaries and contents of carpal tunnel; and
identify the number and compartments of hand muscles and describe the neurovascular bundle of the hand.
courses.contents: Descriptive terms. Plans and terms of relationship of the human body. Terms of comparison. Attachment of muscles. Types of muscles. Movements of joints. Osteology. Principles of Kinesiology. General organisation of body systems. Upper limb. Pectoral region and mammary gland. Axilla and brachial plexus. Deltoid and scapular regions. Arm, forearm, hand, bones and joints.

courses.title: Histology of Basic Tissues
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe the ultrastructure of a cell;
identify the light microscopic features of fibroblasts, chondrocytes, osteocytes, adipocytes, red cells, platelets and red cells;
enumerate the components of extracellular matrix, fibres and ground substance;
identify the collagen and elastic fibres;
state the proteins of the ground substance;
identify the reticuloendothelial system and the various ways of classifying epithelial tissue;
explain the epithelial specialisations of the luminal and abluminal surfaces;
state the differences between microvilli, cilia and stereocilia;
explain the classifications of glands via morphology and method of secretion;
describe the light and electron microscopic pictures of muscle tissue;
state the ultrastructure of a neuron and the basic neuronal types;
explain synapses between neurons and motor end plates;
define myelination of nerve fibres and describe the structure of a peripheral nerve;
enumerate the supporting cells of the neurons centrally and peripherally; and
identify the structure of sense receptors, free nerve endings, Meissner’s and Pacinian corpuscles and muscle spindle.
courses.contents: Components of the cell. Cell cycle. Chromosomes. Protein secretion and transcription of DNA. Introduction to light microscopy. Electron microscopy and units of measurement. Basic tissues of the body. The epithelial, connective and endothelial tissues. Muscle and nervous tissue. Lymphoid organs.

courses.title: General Embryology
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: identify gametogenesis and compare the process in male and female;
classify the hormonal, ovarian and endometrial cycles, and how they are interconnected;
enumerate the preconditions, phases and consequences of fertilization and describe cleavage and implantation;
describe the second week of development as the week of twos, cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, epiblast and hypoblast, somatopleura and splanchnopleure, amniotic and yolk sac cavities;
discuss the establishment of body axes and fate maps during the gastrulation period (third week) and the role of genes in such process;
explain further development of the trophoblast during the third week of development;
identify the derivatives of the three germ layers and how they develop during the embryonic period (third to eighth week); and
describe the development of placenta and fetal membranes.
courses.contents: Gametogenesis. Cyclic changes in the female genital tract. Fertilization, cleavage, blastocyst, gastrulation and formation of germ layers. Segmentation of mesoderm. Folding of embryo foetal membranes. Umbilical cord and placentation. Development of limbs and teratology. Developmental anomalies and their clinical syndromes.

courses.title: Practical Work
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: conduct practicals according to the contents of ANA 201 to 205.
courses.contents: Practical teaching according to the contents of ANA 201 to 205.

courses.title: Introductory Physiology and the Autonomic Nervous System
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe functional organisation of human body;
identify the concept of homeostasis and its failure (illness);
explain control systems of the body;
describe cell membrane and its functions;
recognise various cell organelles and intercellular connections;
describe various mechanisms of transport across cell membrane including active transport, passive transport, simple and facilitated diffusion;
identify the structure neuron and functions;
classify nerve fibres and nerve injury;
classify conduction of nerve impulse, nerve degeneration and regeneration;
describe synapses and neuromuscular junction;
classify muscles;
discuss skeletal muscle contraction and excitation-contraction coupling;
identify smooth muscle contraction;
appreciate nerve conduction studies;
interpret electromyograms (EMG);
explain rigor mortis and contractures;
describe myopathies/neuropathies;
describe functional organisation of autonomic nervous system;
discuss sympathetic division of autonomic nervous system;
discuss parasympathetic division of autonomic nervous system;
outline functions of autonomic nervous system;
enumerate sympathomimetic and sympatholytic drugs; and
list parasympathomimetic and parasympatholytic drugs.
courses.contents: Introduction to physiology and its place in Medicine. The composite cell, cell membrane and transport mechanisms, membrane potentials. Physiology of excitable tissues. Functional organization of autonomic nervous system (ANS). Basic characteristics of sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions. Introduction to human genetics. Biotechnology and human genome.

courses.title: Blood Physiology
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: classify the composition and functions of blood;
enumerate plasma proteins, albumin, globulin fibrinogen, and their functions;
explain red blood cells formation, erythropoiesis, hemoglobin and iron metabolism;
discuss various types of anaemia;
identify blood indices in various disorders, thalassemia;
describe white blood cells formation, leucopoiesis and functions;
discuss platelets, haemostasis, clotting factors and anticoagulants;
explain thrombocytopenia, clotting disorders, haemophilia;
describe the principles of blood grouping and blood transfusion reactions;
explain reticuloendothelial system;
define immunity and its classification;
describe the process of development of cell-mediated immunity;
explain the process of development of humoral immunity;
discuss physiological basis of immunisation; and
describe autoimmune diseases, allergy and immunological hypersensitivity reactions.
courses.contents: General characteristics and functions of blood. Properties and functions of plasma. Red blood cells factors involved in erythropoiesis, blood groups. White blood cells, origin, type, properties, functions, antigenicity and immunities. Platelets and hemostatic mechanisms. Reticulo-endothelial system. Clotting and fibrinolytic systems. Immunity and immunodeficiency disease and HIV.

courses.title: The Cardiovascular System
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: explain the functional organisation of the heart and circulation;
enumerate properties of cardiac muscle and conduction system of the heart;
explain pace-maker potential and artificial pacemaker;
define cardiac cycle and its regulation;
state correlate cardiac cycle;
discuss electrocardiogram (ECG) and heart sounds;
demonstrate ECG-recording and interpretation;
explain mechanism of development of arrhythmias;
classify blood vessels;
explain the mechanism of local control of blood flow;
discuss cardiac output measurement and regulation;
evaluate arterial pulse;
evaluate arterial blood pressure;
explain foetal circulation and readjustments at birth; and
discuss vascular endothelium in cardiovascular control.
courses.contents: Overall plan and functions of the C.V.S. Physiologic anatomy of the heart. Mechanical events of cardiac cycle, cardiac output and its estimation. E.C.G. The Vascular system. Cross sectional area of different vascular groups, systolic, diastolic, pulse and mean pressures, exchange of fluids across the capillaries, venous and central venous pressures. Integration of C.V.S functions, central control centres, regulation of systemic blood pressure. Cardio-vascular adaptations in health and disease. Circulation through special areas. Vascular endothelium in cardiovascular control.

courses.title: Cell Biology, PH and Buffer
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: discuss the role of electro transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation in the generation of ATP;
define genetic;
explain structure of chemistry and function of normal living cell;
discuss metabolism of proteins;
describe carbohydrates, nucleic acids and lipids;
illustrate basic biochemical importance; and
apply biochemical knowledge in the clinics. At the end of this course, students should be able to:
explain classification and chemistry of carbohydrate;
discuss chemistry and biochemistry of the polysaccharide including the amino sugars; mucopolysaccharides, blood group substances;
illustrate structure of chemistry and function of normal living cell;
define metabolism of proteins;
describe carbohydrates, nucleic acids and lipids;
demonstrate basic biochemical importance; and
apply biochemical knowledge in the clinics.
courses.contents: Introduction to Biochemistry. Review of concepts in chemistry applicable to biological systems, chemical bonds covalent and ionic, biomolecules, elementary thermodynamics, reaction equilibria. Henderson equation application. Water, physical, biological and chemical properties. Acid-base chemistry, buffer systems and application to living systems. Introduction of terms used to describe acid-base disorders in the body, academia, alkalemia, acidosis and alkalosis. Enzymes, their properties and kinetics. Diversity of biomolecules, carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, amino acids and nucleic acids in nature. Structure, properties, and biochemical/biological functions of carbohydrates. Lipids, amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids. BCH: 203 Carbohydrate Chemistry (2 Units C: LH 30) Classification and chemistry of carbohydrate. Chemistry and biochemistry of the polysaccharide including the amino sugars, mucopolysaccharides, blood group substances.

courses.title: Amino Acids Chemistry
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: explain chemistry and structure of the amino acids;
classify peptides, essential and non-essential amino acids;
define metabolism of proteins;
describe carbohydrates, nucleic acids and lipids;
illustrate how to apply correctly and interpret the results if different diagnostic test (for example, creatinine, urea, PS) in human diseases; and
apply biochemical knowledge in the clinics.
courses.contents: Chemistry and structure of the amino acids. Peptides, essential and non-essential amino acids.

courses.title: Biochemistry Practical I
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: determine serum electrolyte;
recognise urea;
identify creatinine;
identify serum bilirubin;
recognise uric acid;
classify liver enzymes (ALT, AST and ALP); and
apply biochemical knowledge in the clinics.
courses.contents: Serum electrolyte determination. Urea determination. Creatinine determination. Serum bilirubin determination. Uric acid determination. Serum liver enzymes determination (ALT, AST and ALP).

courses.title: Lipid Metabolism
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: define lipids;
enumerate classification, chemistry and function of lipids;
explain digestion and absorption of lipids in the bloodstream;
identify the lipoproteins; and
apply biochemical knowledge in the clinics.
courses.contents: Introduction to lipids, classification, chemistry and function of lipids. Digestion and absorption of lipids in the bloodstream. The lipoproteins.

courses.title: Clinical Skills I
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: appreciate practical application of knowledge acquired in basic medical and basic clinical sciences;
apply practical knowledge acquired in basic medical and basic clinical sciences;
enhance early clinical exposure;
identify clinical skills; and
emphasise early acquisition of clinical skills.
courses.contents: Clinical application of basic medical and basic clinical sciences. Clinical skills. Principles of courses taught in basic medical and basic clinical science.

courses.title: Philosophy, Logic and Human Existence
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: know the basic features of philosophy as an academic discipline;
identify the main branches of philosophy and the centrality of logic in philosophical discourse;
know the elementary rules of reasoning;
distinguish between valid and invalid arguments;
think critically and assess arguments in texts, conversations and day-to-day discussions;
critically asses the rationality or otherwise of human conduct under different existential conditions;
develop the capacity to extrapolate and deploy expertise in logic to other areas of knowledge; and
guide his or her actions, using the knowledge and expertise acquired in philosophy and logic.
courses.contents: Scope of philosophy, notions, meanings, branches and problems of philosophy. Logic as an indispensable tool of philosophy. Elements of syllogism, symbolic logic-the first nine rules of inference. Informal fallacies, laws of thought, nature of arguments. Valid and invalid arguments, logic of form and logic of content-deduction, induction and inferences. Creative and critical thinking. Impact of philosophy on human existence. Philosophy and politics, philosophy and human conduct, philosophy and religion, philosophy and human values, philosophy and character molding.

courses.title: a: Gross Anatomy of Thorax and Abdomen
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: identify the bones and joints of the thoracic cavity;
differentiate the muscles of respiration in terms of attachment, actions and neurovascular supply;
describe the neurovasculature of the thoracic wall, pleurae, lungs and the tracheobronchial tree;
describe the surfaces, borders, apex, fissures and the root of the lungs;
enumerate the 18-20 bronchopulmonary segments;
explain the layers and neurovascular supply of the pericardium as well as the pericardial space and sinuses;
identify the position, shape, surfaces, base, apex and borders of the heart;
differentiate the external and internal features of the heart chambers;
distinguish the fibrous skeleton and conducting system of the heart;
identify the vascular planes of the branches of the descending aorta;
explain the venous and lymphatics of the thoracic cavity;
describe the course of vagus and phrenic nerves in the thoracic cavity as well as the formation of autonomic nervous plexus in the thorax;
enumerate the course of trachea and oesophagus in the thoracic cavity;
list the attachments, actions and neurovascular supply of the diaphragm;
explain the divisions and communications of the peritoneal cavity;
identify the external and internal features as well as the neurovascular supply of the abdominal oesophagus; stomach, small and large intestine;
identify the external features, surfaces, borders and relations of the liver;
explain the parts of the gallbladder, its relations and neurovascular supply as well the extrahepatic biliary tree;
list the parts, relations and neurovascular supply of the pancreas;
describe the surfaces, borders, relations and neurovascular supply of the spleen;
identify the attachments of the renal fascia; and
discuss the relations and neurovascular supply of the kidneys and the suprarenal glands.
courses.contents: Thorax, thoracic wall, pleura, lungs. Heart and coronary vessels mediastinum and diaphragm. Abdomen, anterior abdominal wall, external genitalia, peritoneum, stomach and intestines, blood supply. Liver and gall bladder, pancreas, spleen, kidneys and suprarenal. Pelvis and surface anatomy. Radiological anatomy.

courses.title: b: Gross Anatomy of Pelvis and Perineum
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: enumerate the three bones forming the wall of the pelvic cavity;
explain the articular surfaces and ligaments of the sacroiliac and lumbosacral joints as well as those of pubic symphysis;
identify the boundaries and planes of pelvic inlet and outlet as well as the axis of the pelvic cavity;
distinguish the various pelvic diameters and pelvic types;
describe the attachments, actions and neurovascular supply of the muscles forming the floor, lateral and posterior walls of the pelvic cavity;
identify the endopelvic fascia and its condensations;
enumerate the external and internal features of the rectum as well as its neurovascular supply;
list the external and internal features of the urinary bladder and its neurovascular supply;
describe the relations and neurovasculature of prostate;
explain the relations, external and internal features of the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina as well as their neurovasculature;
identify the divisions of perineum;
explain the male external genitalia and their neurovascular supply;
explain the female external genitalia and their microvasculature; and
discuss the boundaries and contents of ischiorectal fossa.
courses.contents: Perineum. Male and female perineum. Pelvic wall and floor. Pelvic peritoneum. Pelvic viscera. Sympathetic and parasympathetic neurovascular structures. Surface anatomy. Radiological anatomy.

courses.title: Systemic Histology (Organology)
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: define the ultrastructure of a cell;
describe the light microscopic features of fibroblasts, chondrocytes, osteocytes, adipocytes, red cells, platelets and red cells;
identify the collagen and elastic fibres;
define the proteins of the ground substance;
describe the light microscopic features of the three heart layers including histology of the conducting system;
conduct the light microscopy of the elastic, muscular arteries and arterioles;
list the ultrastructure of the three types of endothelia;
identify the structure of veins;
explain the structure of lymphatic vessels and lymphoid organs including spleen;
describe the light microscopic picture of skin layers and structure of its appendages.;
explain the peculiarities of the thick skin of palms and soles;
describe the basic structure of the respiratory epithelium;
explain the structure of olfactory epithelium;
illustrate the basic arrangement of structures in the wall of airway;
describe the ultrastructure of blood-air barrier;
discuss the basic organisation of the wall of the gastrointestinal tract;
describe the light microscopic structure of all the different parts of the digestive tract;
describe the light microscopic structure of liver, pancreas and biliary tree;
explain the light microscopic structure of the different segments of nephron;
illustrate the ultrastructure of the glomerulus and the filtration barrier;
conduct the light microscopy of the prostate, erectile bodies and prepuce;
describe the light microscopic picture of the ovarian and endometrial cycles;
explain the light microscopic picture of the cervix and vagina;
describe female breast in various stages of development;
describe the light microscopic structure of the auricle, ear drum and membrane lining the tympanic cavity;
explain the light microscopic picture of the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear including the maculae, cristae and organ or Corti;
describe the light microscopic picture of eyelids, conjunctivae and the lens; and
list the layers of the eyeball and the layers of retina.
courses.contents: Cardiovascular system. Skin, gland of the skin. Structure of the nails and hair. Respiratory system. Digestive system. Neurological system. Musculo-skeletal system. Urinary and genital systems. Electron micrograph studies of each organ.

courses.title: Systemic Embryology (Organogenesis)
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe gametogenesis and compare the process in male and female;
appraise the hormonal, ovarian and endometrial cycles and how they are interconnected;
list the preconditions, phases and consequences of fertilization;
describe cleavage and implantation;
explain the second week of development as the week of twos, cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, epiblast and hypoblast, somatopleura and splanchnopleure, amniotic and yolk sac cavities;

discuss the establishment of body axes and fate maps during the gastrulation period (third week) and the role of genes in such process and illustrate the further development of the trophoblast during the third week of development;
discuss the derivatives of the three germ layers and how they develop during the embryonic period (third to eighth week); and
describe the development of placenta and fetal membranes.
courses.contents: Development of cardiovascular system, integumentary system, respiratory system, digestive system, urogenital system, nervous system. Developmental anomalies and their clinical syndromes.

courses.title: Practical Work
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: conduct practicals according to the contents of ANA 202 to 206.
courses.contents: Practical teaching according to the contents of ANA 202 to 206.

courses.title: Renal Physiology, Body Fluids and Temperature Regulation
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe the structure of kidney and nephron;
list general functions of kidney;
describe GFR and factors regulating it;
explain the process of urine formation, filtration, reabsorption and secretion;
discuss the processes producing concentrated and diluted urine;
describe the regulation of blood pressure by kidneys;
list the hormones of kidney;
define acidification of urine;
conduct renal function tests;
discuss renal failure and haemodialysis; and
describe micturition reflex and abnormalities of micturition including incontinence.
courses.contents: The skin. Functional anatomy, temperature regulations, abnormalities of temperature regulation. Metabolism, factors regulating metabolism, conditions for measuring basal metabolic rate. Compartmentalization and composition of body fluids. Physiologic anatomy of the kidney, renal circulation and autoregulation. Glomerular filtration. Tubular transport. Urine formation, counter-current system. Water volume and ionic regulation. Acid-base balance. Micturition. Abnormalities of renal function.

courses.title: Respiratory System
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe the functional organisation of respiratory tract;
outline functions of lungs, respiratory and non-respiratory;
explain the mechanics of breathing;
discuss the role of surfactant compliance;
describe lung volumes and capacities;
discuss respiratory changes during exercise, mechanism of sneezing, yawning, cough;
explain obstructive/restrictive lung disease, FEV1/FVC;
differentiate types of respiratory failure, types I and II, artificial respiration; and
explain oxygen therapy and its toxicity.
courses.contents: Physiologic anatomy of respiratory apparatus. Brief review of relevant gas laws. Lung volumes. Mechanics of breathing. Gas diffusion through alveoli, capillary membrane. Pulmonary circulation, ventilation perfusion ratio. O2 and CO2 transport. Control of respiration, hypoxias, O2 treatment, abnormal types of breathing. Altitude and depth acclimatization. Respiratory adjustments in health and disease. Aerospace physiology. Deep sea diving.

courses.title: Neuroscience I
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe the functional organisation of nervous system;
classify nerve fibres;
describe the properties of synaptic transmission;
outline neurotransmitters and neuropeptides;
classify types and functions of sensory receptors;
describe structure and functions of spinal cord;
identify reflex action and other reflexes;
describe muscle spindle and muscle tone, tactile, temperature and pain sensations;
explain the structure and functions of cerebral cortex;
describe motor pathways (pyramidal and extra pyramidal);
discuss basal ganglia, its connections and functions;
describe cerebellum, its connections and functions;
explain vestibular apparatus and regulation of posture and equilibrium, physiology of sleep and sleep disorders;
describe electroencephalogram (EEG) Physiology of memory, physiology of speech and its bnormalities;
identify thalamus- nuclei, functions and thalamic syndrome;
describe hypothalamus and limbic system;
explain analgesia system of the body, disorders of cranial nerves; and
describe higher mental function assessment.
courses.contents: Development and general plan of the central nervous system. Nerve morphology, generation and conduction of action potential. Sensory division of the nervous system, morphology receptors, sensory pathways, reticular formation, thalamus and sensory cortex.

courses.title: Nucleic Acids Chemistry
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe genome organisation and biosynthesis of proteins;
explain metabolism of purines and pyrimidines, nucleosides and nucleotides;
identify abnormalities in nucleic acid metabolism-xeroderma pigmentation and skin cancer;
explain overview of nitrogen metabolism;
define biosynthesis of amino acids and identify molecules derived from amino acids and biosynthesis;
discuss degradation of nucleotides; and
apply biochemical knowledge in the clinics.
courses.contents: Genome organisation and biosynthesis of proteins. Metabolism of purines and pyrimidines, nucleosides and nucleotides. Abnormalities in nucleic acid metabolism-xeroderma pigmentation and skin cancer. Overview of nitrogen metabolism, biosynthesis of amino acids. Molecules derived from amino acids and biosynthesis and degradation of nucleotides.

courses.title: Enzymes, Coenzymes and Bioenergetics
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: define enzymes and enumerate functions, nature and properties of enzymes;
describe kinetics of enzyme action;
enumerate allosteric effects;
explain enzyme assay in clinical medicine and immobilised enzymes;
identify hybridoma technology and monoclonal antibodies in medicine and biological research;
discuss the role of electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation in the generation of ATP, theories and models proposed for ATP generation; and
apply biochemical knowledge in the clinic.
courses.contents: Introduction to enzymes. Properties and functions, nature and properties of enzymes. Kinetics of enzyme action, allosteric effects. Enzyme assay in clinical medicine, immobilised enzymes, hybridoma technology and monoclonal antibodies in medicine and biological research. The role of electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation in the generation of ATP, theories and models proposed for ATP generation.

courses.title: Amino Acids Metabolism
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: define the metabolism of amino acid;
outline transamination, oxidative deamination, decarboxylation;
discuss the urea cycle and its biochemical importance;
explain inborn errors of metabolism of some amino acids;
outline phenylketonuria, tyrosinosis, alkaptonuria, albinism, cystinuria; and
apply biochemical knowledge in the clinics.
courses.contents: Introduction to the metabolism of amino acid. Transamination, oxidative deamination, decarboxylation. The urea cycle and its biochemical importance’s. Inborn errors of metabolism of some amino acids, phenylketonuria, tyrosinosis, alkaptonuria, albinism, cystinuria.

courses.title: Carbohydrate Metabolism
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: outline glycolysis (Embden- Meyerhof pathway), aerobic and anaerobic phases;
explain the control mechanisms and substrate level phosphorylation;
illustrate the kerb’s cycle/citric acid cycle;
discuss metabolism of galactose and fructose the uronic acid pathway gluconeogenesis, glycogenesis and glycogenolysis;
explain the HMP shunt and its biochemical importance; and
apply biochemical knowledge in the clinics.
courses.contents: Glycolysis (Embden- Meyerhof pathway), aerobic and anaerobic phases. Control mechanisms and substrate level phosphorylation. The kerb’s cycle/citric acid cycle. Metabolism of galactose and fructose the uronic acid pathway gluconeogenesis, glycogenesis and glycogenolysis. The HMP shunt and its biochemical importance.

courses.title: Biochemistry Practical II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: explain practical and theoretical knowledge of the biochemical basis of human diseases;
describe serum cholesterol determination;
illustrate lipoprotein determination;
demonstrate an understanding of the nature, properties and clinical importance of enzymes;
interpret the results of different diagnostic test in human diseases; and
apply biochemical knowledge in the clinics.
courses.contents: Serum cholesterol determination. Lipoprotein determination.

courses.title: Multidisciplinary Healthcare
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe the inter-relationship between the different healthcare professionals;
outline complimentary roles in healthcare delivery;
discuss a broad based knowledge in applied medical sciences and an early orientation to multidisciplinary healthcare delivery;
appreciate early orientation to multidisciplinary healthcare delivery;
prioritise unity team approach to patient care; and
define basic medical terms and components of the medical interview.
courses.contents: Moral Philosophy. Clinical ethics and professionalism. Communication/interviewing skills healthcare delivery as an inter-disciplinary profession. Human resource for health. Introduction to the roles of various healthcare specialists in MHD, complimentary and alternate Medicine, human Nutrition, critical care medicine, psychology, complementary and Alternative Medicine. Herbal and traditional medicine. Spiritual medicine. Energy and mind-body medicine. Biologically based medical practice. Public health aspects of CAM. Medical jurisprudence and professional liability issues.

courses.title: Clinical Skills II
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: appreciate practical application of knowledge acquired in basic medical and basic clinical sciences;
apply practical knowledge acquired in basic medical and basic clinical sciences;
develop early clinical exposure;
identify clinical skills; and
recognise early acquisition of clinical skills.
courses.contents: Clinical application of basic medical and basic clinical sciences. Clinical skills. Principles of courses taught in basic medical and basic clinical science. 300 Level

courses.title: Gross Anatomy of Head and Neck and Neuroanatomy
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: describe the features of the cervical vertebrae and articulations between them;
discuss the articular surfaces, ligaments and movements of the atlantooccipital and atlantoaxial joints;
identify the parts of hyoid bone;
outline the different layers of the cervical fasciae and their attachments;
differentiate the boundaries and contents of different regions and triangles of the neck;
explain the formation and the sensory and motor branches of the cervical plexus of nerves;
identify the structures of the root of the neck and describe the external features and neurovascular supply of thyroid gland;
discuss how the different cartilages, ligaments and muscles of the larynx articulate and attach to produce the whole structure;
describe the neurovascular supply to the larynx;
explain the attachments of constrictors and inner longitudinal layer of the pharynx as well as their neurovasculature;
identify the internal features of the different parts of the pharynx;
describe the different surfaces of articulated neuro- and viscerocranium and illustrate the layers of scalp;
list the muscles of face around the orbital, nasal and oral orifices in terms of attachments and functions; and
discuss the neurovasculature of the scalp and face.
courses.contents: Head and neck. Face and scalp. Back and spinal cord. Cranial cavity. Orbit, parotid, temporal and infratemporal regions. Triangles of neck, submandibular region, nerves and vessels in deep dissection of neck. Thyroid and parathyroid. Pre-vertebral region and joints of neck. Mouth and tongue, pharynx, palato-nasal cavity and sinuses, larynx, ear and eye. Neuroanatomy. Meninges, base of brain and blood supply, hindbrain, medulla, pons, cerebellum and 4th ventricle, midbrain, diencephalon and third ventricle, cerebral hemispheres, sulci and gyri, internal structure of cerebrum and lateral ventricle, basal nuclei, thalamus and hypothalamus, synapses and reflex arcs. Sensory and ascending pathways, motor and descending pathways, cerebellar connections-pathways for hearing, smell and vision. Autonomic nervous system. Radiological and applied anatomy of the Head and Neck. Brain and spinal cord.

courses.title: Histology of Special Senses and Neuro-Histology/Histo-Chemistry
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: define the ultrastructure of a cell;
describe the light microscopic features of fibroblasts, chondrocytes, osteocytes, adipocytes, red cells, platelets and red cells;
explain the collagen and elastic fibres;
describe the proteins of the ground substance;
define the reticuloendothelial system;
discuss the various ways of classifying epithelial tissue;
outline the epithelial specialisations of the luminal and abluminal surfaces;
differentiate between microvilli, cilia and stereocilia;
explain the classifications of glands via morphology and method of secretion;
describe the light and electron microscopic pictures of muscle tissue;
identify synapses between neurons and motor end plates;
define myelination of nerve fibres and describe the structure of a peripheral nerve;
outline the supporting cells of the neurons centrally and peripherally;
explain the structure of sense receptors, free nerve endings, Meissner’s and Pacinian corpuscles and muscle spindle;
describe the light microscopic features of the three heart layers including histology of the conducting system;
demonstrate the light microscopy of the elastic, muscular arteries and arterioles;
enumerate the ultrastructure of the three types of endothelia;
define the structure of veins;
describe the structure of lymphatic vessels and lymphoid organs including spleen;
discuss the light microscopic picture of skin layers and structure of its appendages;
outline the peculiarities of the thick skin of palms and soles;
describe the basic structure of the respiratory epithelium;
define the structure of olfactory epithelium;
explain the basic arrangement of structures in the wall of airway;
discuss the light microscopic picture of the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear including the maculae, cristae and organ or Corti;
describe the light microscopic picture of eyelids, conjunctivae and the lens;
identify the layers of the eyeball;
state the layers of retina;
describe stained sections of the spinal cord and brainstem at various levels; and
distinguish the cortical layers of the cerebrum and cerebellum.
courses.contents: Neurohistology. Spinal cord, brain stem, cerebrum and cerebellum. Organs of special senses, sensory receptors, eyes, ear and nose. Histology of endocrine organs. Principles and techniques of histochemistry including immunocytochemistry.

courses.title: Neuro-Embryology and Development of Pharyngeal Apparatus
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: explain gametogenesis and compare the process in male and female;
describe the hormonal, ovarian and endometrial cycles and how they are interconnected;
outline the preconditions, phases and consequences of fertilization;
describe cleavage and implantation;
discuss the establishment of body axes and fate maps during the gastrulation period, third week and the role of genes in such process;
explain further development of the trophoblast during the third week of development;
outline the derivatives of the three germ layers and how they develop during the embryonic period, third to eighth week;
describe the development of placenta and fetal membranes;
explain the development of membranous and cartilaginous neurocranium;
describe the development of the limbs and the vertebral column;
outline the development of cardiac loop, sinus venosus as well as cardiac septa;
describe the development of aortic arches and the venous system;
explain fetal circulation and the transition happening after birth;
describe the development of the respiratory bud and the origins of the respiratory epithelium, smooth muscle and cartilages;
discuss the formation of body cavity and the diaphragm;
describe the developments of the derivatives of the foregut, its artery as well as dorsal and ventral mesentry;
outline the development of the midgut, its rotation and its artery and dorsal mesentry;
describe the development of the hindgut;
explain the developments of the three systems of kidneys and that of the excretory and collecting system of the kidneys;
describe the developments of bladder in urethra from the upper and pelvic parts of the urogenital sinus and contrast the process in males and females;
explain and compare and contrast the development of gonads and genital tracts in males and females and explain the role of genes and hormones in this process;
compare and contrast the development of external genitalia in males and females and the roles of genes and hormones in this process;
outline the derivatives of the pharyngeal arches, pouches and clefts;
explain the developments and origins of the three parts of the ear; and
describe the development of eyelids, conjunctival sac, lens vesicle and eyeball.
courses.contents: Development of the face, pharyngeal derivatives and teratology. Development of nervous system and sense organs. Developmental anomalies and their clinical syndromes.

courses.title: Human Genetics
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: explain the chromosome theory of inheritance;
describe the process of cell division; mitotic and meiotic;
appreciate introduction to karyotyping and cytogenetic analysis techniques;
explain how abnormalities in chromosome number and structure arise;
define single gene mutations; and
identify the phenotypic expressions of some selected chromosomal and single gene mutation abnormalities.
courses.contents: Fundamental human genetic principles. Variation in gene expression in man. Patterns of inheritances in families (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked dominant, X- linked recessive, Y-linked and sex influenced). Cytogenetics, types and classification of human chromosomes. Methods of preparation of human chromosomes and Karyotyping. Types of numerical and structural chromosome aberrations and their causes. Gene hybridisation. Human genomic studies.

courses.title: Laboratory Techniques for Light Microscopy/Gross Radiologic Techniques
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate the practical step by step method of tissue processing for light microscope study;
demonstrate the principles and techniques for the use of advance light microscopes;
classify polarising microscope, phase contrast microscope, interference microscope, dark- field microscope and ultraviolet microscope;
discuss basic principles of radiological imaging of human tissue;
identify radiological of major body structures;
appreciate introduction to modern imaging techniques; and
state precautionary measures.
courses.contents: The practical step by step method of tissue processing for light microscope study shall be taught and demonstrated. The principles and techniques for the use of advance light microscopes will be taught and where possible demonstrated. Polarising microscope. Phase contrast microscope. Interference microscope. Dark-Field microscope, and ultraviolet microscope. Basic principles of radiological imaging of human tissue. Radiological identification of major body structures. Introduction to modern imaging techniques. Precautionary measures.

courses.title: Practical Work
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: identify organs, tissues and other structures in the head and neck region;
trace cause and relation of various structures and organs in the head and neck;
recognise variations in location and relation of anatomical structures in the head and neck;
demonstrate dissection techniques; and
and recognise histological patterns of head and neck tissues.
courses.contents: Practical work in line with the principles of ANA 301 to 307.

courses.title: Gastrointestinal Physiology
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: outline different parts of the GIT and their functions;
define the enteric nervous system;
explain the processes of mastication and swallowing and their control;
enumerate functions and movements of stomach, small intestine and large intestine;
list hormones of GIT and their functions;
discuss vomiting and its pathway;
explain the process of defecation and its pathway; and
discuss regulation of feeding and energy expenditure.
courses.contents: Physiologic anatomy of the gastrointestinal tract. Review of smooth muscle function. Secretions in the G.I.T. and their control. Movements of the gastrointestinal tract. Digestion and absorption of various food substances. Liver and its functions. Disorders of G.I.T. The Gut as an endocrine organ.

courses.title: Endocrinology and Reproduction
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: outline general principles (classification, mechanism of action, feedback control) of hormones;
describe physiology of growth;
define calcium metabolism and glucose metabolism;
describe the functional anatomy of male reproductive system;
discuss spermatogenesis and semen analysis, erection and ejaculation;
discuss testosterone and male puberty;
describe the functional anatomy of female reproductive system, gonads and oogenesis;
discuss oestrogen and progesterone;
explain menstrual cycle, puberty and menopause;
describe the physiological changes in mother’s body during pregnancy;
discuss physiology of parturition and lactation;
define contraception;
interpret pregnancy tests; and
discuss assisted fertility techniques.
courses.contents: Endocrine system. Introduction and neuroendocrine relationship. Hypothalamo-pituitary axis, Endocrine glands, normal, hypo- and hyper-functions. Other hormones of some clinical importance. Physiologic anatomy of male and female reproductive system. Male and female sex hormones. Cyclicity of hormone secretion in females. Physiology of contraception. Assisted fertility techniques.

courses.title: Pathophysiology I
courses.outcomes_intro: At the end of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: outline causes and mechanism of cellular adaptations, cell injury, cell death and apoptosis, cancer and aging;
describe the aetiology and pathogenesis of anaemias;
state disorders of haemostasis;
explain blood transfusion and its complications;
outline autoimmune diseases, allergy and immunological hypersensitivity reactions;
state and describe disorders of peripheral circulation;
describe disorders of cardiac rhythm and conduction;
outline the pathophysiology of heart failure, hypertension and ischemic heart disease;
differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary diseases;
discuss pulmonary arterial hypertension and pulmonary oedema;
explain nephritic and nephrotic syndrome;
describe the pathophysiology of acute and chronic renal failure;
discuss tetany and pathophysiology of cramps; and
define acidosis and alkalosis. At the end of this course, students should be able to:
develop an opportunity to review the physiological concept of systems taught;
outline thoroughly the physiological concept of systems taught; and
demonstrate the concept using available equipment to medical or junior physiology students.
courses.contents: Introduction to pathophysiology. Cellular response to persistent stress, adaptations hyperplasia, hypertrophy, metaplasia, atrophy, intracellular accumulations, cell injury death and senescence mechanisms of cell injury, programmed cell death and necrosis, cellular ageing. Pathophysiology of prolonged bleeding time, purpura, haemophilia, hemoglobinopathies, pathophysiology of sickle cell disease, thalassemia, hypersplenism. Pathophysiology of anaemia, megaloblastic anaemia, pathophysiology erythroblastosis fetalis, incompatible blood transfusion. Pathophysiology of palpitation, cardiac arrhythmia, heart block, angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, murmurs, pathophysiology of heart failure, hypertension, Reynold’s disease, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary oedema, pulmonary hypertensions and cor pulmonale. Pathophysiology of cerebral blood flow disturbance (stroke), pathophysiology oedema and lymphedema, pathophysiology of syncope and postural hypotension. Respiratory distress syndrome, Pathophysiology of haemothorax hydrothorax and pneumothorax.
